title: Scandinavian Stars Bjerre, Haug Join Martinez In 3 0 Thursday Triumph
summary:
GM Jonas Buhl Bjerre, IM Havard Haug, and GM Jose Martinez were all outright victors of the November 26 3 0 Thursday events, each winning with commanding scores of 10/11.

Bjerre's win was particularly special as it was his first title, and the first by any Danish player. For Haug and Martinez, the victories marked their second and 16th, respectively.

First Tournament: Bjerre, The Cat With Nine Lives

In the first tournament of the day, Bjerre did his best impression of Harry Houdini, somehow escaping from completely lost positions on no less than four occasions.

Bjerre weaseled his way out of trouble against FM Sergey Borischik, GM Dmitry Andreikin, IM Renato Terry, and GM Zhamsaran Tsydypov.

Bjerre almost came unstuck against Borischik in the first round after the latter steered the game into a winning rook and pawn ending. However, Bjerre held on long enough for Borischik's time to become an issue, and flag fall eventually decided the game.

Bjerre (pictured on the right) used the clock as a weapon throughout the entire event. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Chess.com.

In a round six showdown with Terry, Bjerre had his closest call. With 2.6 seconds left on the clock, Terry uncharacteristically missed checkmate in one, instead throwing his queen into the line of fire of Bjerre's rooks. Clearly perplexed by the mistake, Bjerre took almost a full second to capture the queen, before also flagging Terry.

One of Bjerre's main challengers was GM Oleksandr Bortnyk, who came face-to-face with the leader in round eight. By this stage, however, the Danish GM was firing on all cylinders. In the late middlegame, he put the game to bed with the astute 34.Rxe7!!.

By the final round, Bjerre had guaranteed a share of first place, and a draw with GM Denis Lazavik confirmed a one point winning margin. Tsydypov, finished in second with 9/11, besting GMs Lazavik and Liem Le Quang on tiebreaks. WIM Meri Arabidze was the top scoring women's player with 7.5/11.

The top 10 finishers in the second tournament.

Second Tournament: Haug Miles Ahead

Haug's performance in the second tournament was nothing short of breathtaking. He barely put a foot wrong en route to an 8/8 start, frequently capitalizing on opponents' time-pressure-induced mistakes late in the game.

The 16-year-old steamrolled his first eight opponents and then cruised to victory.

Polish GM Zbigniew Pakleza become one of the victims of Haug's opportunism in round three after he blundered a key pawn in an opposite-colored bishop endgame.

In the following game, GM Vladimir Fedoseev was put to the sword in a similar fashion in a rook vs. rook endgame. 16 moves from the 50-move-rule and with 13 seconds on the clock, Fedoseev erred with 98...Rf6??, allowing Haug to acquire an extra half point from the clash.

Having accumulated a half point lead by the eighth round, Haug played it safe with draws in the ninth and 10th rounds, before asserting his dominance by flagging GM David Paravyan.

With wins in the final round, GM Matthias Bluebaum and FM Dincer Tasdogen finished on 8.5/11 and snuck into second and third place, respectively. Meanwhile, Ukrainian NM Ivanytska Liudmyla secured the top women's prize for her 17th place finish.

The top 10 finishers in the second tournament.

Third Tournament: Martinez Just Shy Of Perfect Performance

The third tournament was a one-man show from start to finish, featuring the now-16 time winner Martinez. 10 consecutive victories left him on the brink of achieving the first perfect score in 3 0 Thursday history. However, a tough loss on the black side of the Queen's Pawn Opening: Levitsky Attack at the hands of Terry denied him the accolade.

Terry spoiled the perfect points party. Photo: Renato Terry.

Martinez's earlier games stood out due to his lightning pace and incisive sacrifices. In round 10, he punched a hole in Fedoseev's kingside with the delectable 18.Nxe6!!.

Wins over GMs Sina Movahed, Volodar Murzin, and IM Yoseph Taher further underlined the dominance of his performance.

Martinez knocked over 3000+ rated blitzers like bowling pins. Photo: Chess.com.

Martinez wasn't the only player racking up brilliancies, though. The top scoring women's player, Bulgarian IM Nurgyul Salimova, climed to 12th place after uncorking a sacrifice that directed the game towards a winning rook ending.

When the dust settled, Martinez finished first with 10/11, Movahed in second on 9/11, and GM Nguyen Ngoc Truong Son in third with 8.5/11.

The top 10 finishers in the third tournament.

3 0 Thursday is a set of three weekly Swiss tournaments for verified titled players featuring their favorite time control. Each of the three tournaments is an 11-round Swiss with a 3+0 time control. The combined prize fund is $3,000 every week.

title: Salesforce FIDE World Championship, Game 3: A tense fight ends in a draw
summary: The third game of the Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026 in Geneva ended in a draw after a 60-move battle. The match is tied at 1½–1½ heading into the rest day. The ceremonial first move was made by Mike Klein, Chess.com Senior Journalist and Content Creator, who is also representing Chess.com on site as one of the official partners of the World Championship. Having polled his colleagues beforehand about which first move should be played, he found that the vast majority favoured 1.f4. It is unlikely, though, that Sindarov ever considered playing the Bird Opening in the match, so he went for 1.e4 once again. Gukesh sprang the first surprise of the day, deviating from the course of the first game with the slightly unusual 5…Be7, known as the Rio de Janeiro Variation of the Berlin Defence in the Ruy Lopez. This move was frequently played towards the end of the 19th century and was later ventured from time to time in top-level encounters. One may notably recall the second game of the 1981 World Championship match, when Korchnoi tried to catch Karpov off guard with it, albeit without success. Sindarov needed some time to recover from this surprise and try to recall his preparation. Presumably, he had not looked at this particular line during his morning preparation and therefore had to rely on work he might have done several months earlier. In any case, the Uzbek challenger followed a promising line, including the interesting 12.Nc3, which had only been played in three earlier games. Gukesh continued to follow his preparation until 16.b3, after which he took a long time before deciding to exchange queens. The sequence that followed might have given the impression that Black had seized the initiative, but 22.Nc5+ led to an endgame with opposite-coloured bishops. The drawish nature of this type of endgame is well known, but with all rooks still on the board, both players felt there was plenty left to fight for. According to the players, a critical moment arose after Gukesh moved his bishop from f5 to c4, a manoeuvre he was not happy with in hindsight.  This allowed White to launch a kingside pawn break with the attractive 29.f4. Sindarov, however, felt afterwards that he had rushed into this move and should first have prepared it with 29.h3. Gukesh admitted at the press conference that he had overlooked f4. His acute sense of danger helped him find a safe way to maintain the balance. A scary moment came for Sindarov just before the time control. Eager to calculate every detail, he let his clock run down to just eight seconds before playing his 40th move. Luckily for him, the position had become sufficiently simplified, and he was able to play his final move before the time control without hesitation. It is worth recalling that both players are given two hours for the first 40 moves. A 30-second increment per move is only added from move 41 onwards, when both players also receive an extra 30 minutes to finish the game. In the final phase, Sindarov defended accurately, and the players eventually shook hands on the 60th move. Friday, 27 November, is the first rest day in Cologny. The players will certainly use at least part of the day to recharge their batteries, while their teams get back to work in search of new ideas for the upcoming encounter. We can look forward to an exciting weekend, with the fourth game scheduled to start at 3 p.m. on Saturday, November 28, at the Fondation Martin Bodmer. FACT SHEET – Game 3, Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026 White: Javokhir Sindarov Black: Gukesh Dommaraju Result: ½–½ Opening: Ruy Lopez, Berlin Defence Game length: 60 moves Match score: 1½–1½ Two events were on the programme in the Fan Zone today. First, six-time Swiss champion Yannick Pelletier played friendly blitz games against members of the public. The grandmaster played all his games with Black, winning all but one, which ended in a draw. Later in the afternoon, Anna Muzychuk provided commentary on the ongoing World Championship game for the audience and answered numerous questions from the fans. This kind of interaction is greatly appreciated by the public, as it helps demystify top players and make them more approachable. Written by Yannick Pelletier Photos: Y.E. Nisenbaum and Michal Walusza The Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026 is taking place at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, near Geneva, Switzerland, from November 22 to December 12. All information on the schedule can be found on the Championship website. Tickets to the playing hall and the fan zone can be purchased on the designated website: https://tickets.fide.com/en , while games can be watched on the FIDE YouTube channel with live commentaries by top Grandmasters Peter Leko and Peter Svidler.

title: World Championship Game 3: A lively draw ahead of the first rest day
summary:
A third consecutive draw was seen at the World Chess Championship in Geneva on Thursday, though game three was the longest and the most engaging encounter of the match so far. Gukesh Dommaraju demonstrated the depth of his preparation in a different line of the Berlin Defence, while Javokhir Sindarov dealt admirably with an uncomfortable position and severe time pressure. The match remains level going into Friday's rest day. | Photo: FIDE / Michal Walusza

Shifts in momentum

A third draw in as many games was seen in Geneva on Thursday, but the encounter that preceded the first rest day of the World Championship match was both the longest and the one that featured the most shifts in momentum. For the first time in the match, it was Gukesh Dommaraju who clearly had the upper hand in the opening preparation, while Javokhir Sindarov demonstrated his ability to deal with a difficult practical situation.

Sindarov, playing white for the second time in the match, again opened with 1.e4, and Gukesh once again opted for the Berlin Defence with 1...e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 . The defending champion deviated from game one, however, by following 4.0-0 Nxe4 5.d4 with 5...Be7 , i.e. the Rio de Janeiro Variation ( as Anish Giri pointed out , the World Championship contenders have already "visited" Berlin, London and Rio!).

The difference in the quality - or depth - of the players' preparation became particularly apparent after Gukesh's rather unusual 8...Nf5 , with 8...Nb7 accounting for close to 90% of the games played from the position.

Sindarov spent six and nine minutes on his next two moves, respectively, while Gukesh continued to play quickly.

Interestingly, the contenders were following in the footsteps of two chess legends. All the moves up to and including 13...Qb8 had been seen in an encounter between Ljubomir Ljubojevic and Boris Spassky at the 1988 World Cup in Belfort, France. That game ended in a draw, although Spassky needed to show his defensive skills to hold the position with black.

Sindarov introduced a novelty with 14.a3 , by which point he was already 40 minutes behind on the clock and clearly finding his moves over the board. Gukesh blitzed out two more moves, making it clear that he had studied the position in considerable depth.

The queens left the board by move 17, but the resulting position was rich in possibilities, with notable imbalances in pawn structure and piece activity.

Game three unfolding at the Fondation Martin Bodmer | Photo: Y.E. Nisenbaum

What followed was a fine illustration of the strengths of the two young grandmasters. Gukesh kept looking for ways to increase the pressure, gaining space on the kingside and finding a number of subtle manoeuvres, while Sindarov had to deal with an uncomfortable position and a sizeable deficit on the clock, having been outprepared for the first time in the match.

A crucial moment came when Sindarov played 29.f4 , breaking on the kingside. While the Uzbek grandmaster was rather critical of his decision at the post-game press conference, Gukesh explained that he had overlooked this particular break, despite expecting his opponent to seek counterplay on that flank.

The Indian spent over 15 minutes on his response - his longest think of the game. Although the engines continued to assess the position as equal, Black had seemingly lost some of the momentum, as active plans were now harder to come by. If anything, it was Sindarov who had the slightly more promising position.

At that point, was also plenty of tension surrounding the clock situation, with Sindarov having to play at a pace of roughly one minute per move. Remarkably, the precision of play hardly suffered, even as the challenger made his 40 th move with just six seconds to spare.

By the time the players reached the time control, an endgame with rooks and bishops of opposite colours had arisen.

There was still work to be done to maintain the balance, and the contenders continued playing until move 60, when they agreed to a draw.

The match thus remains level at 1½–1½ going into Friday's rest day. While neither player has yet managed to secure a win, Thursday's game offered a glimpse of the sort of prolonged, strategically complex battles we might see as the match progresses.

Sindarov ½-½ Gukesh

title: When chess starts to sing
summary:
How ChessBase 27 turns the World Championship into a musical experience. It all started with Ask ChessBase, a fascinating new concept in ChessBase 27 - an AI assistant that has access to the functionality of the chess program it lives in. You can ask it almost anything about the current position or a game. We used it to create musicals about chess.

One thing it is particularly good at is annotating games. It relies on ChessBase's trusted Tactical Analysis for concrete variations, but then goes a significant step further: it explains the game in natural language, describing ideas and turning points. It tells the story of a game.

Playing around with this, we discovered that it is also quite clever at solving the funny task “Write song lyrics about this game”. The resulting lyrics can capture the essence of a game remarkably well. They describe the dramatic moments and the emotion of the players.

Of course, song lyrics are not yet a song. But today there are plenty of AI tools that can turn lyrics into music, in almost any musical style. Working with these tools feels a little like the early days of AI image generation. You have to experiment with prompts, try different styles, and be patient until something really good emerges. But the results can be delightful.

Everything described so far is something you can try yourself with ChessBase 27. We decided to take the idea two steps further.

First , we developed a system that visualizes the music on a chessboard. As you listen to the song, you can follow the moves and see the chess story unfold. The music and the game become a single experience. You may have already seen this in the opening articles of ChessBase 27 .

Second , we built an authoring system based on Ask ChessBase that can write the script for an entire mini-musical about a game.

The original "Ask ChessBase" analysis of the first game in the world championship that led to the script of the musical

Covering a whole chess game in one single song would either be a very long and winding road or miss a lot of important details. So one needs several songs, usually three or four to cover one game. Add an introduction, a few spoken interludes, and a conclusion, and this gets you a complete little musical with a natural dramatic structure.

Multiple songs also allow for musical variety and different perspectives. Chess may have only two players, but they make excellent protagonists. One may be confident and ambitious, the other cautious or defiant.

A third voice, perhaps a female spectator or commentator, can observe the struggle and reflect on what the players themselves fail to see. This creates opportunities for contrasting musical styles.

And that is enough to turn a chess game into a small theatrical story in which the moves provide the plot and the players become characters. The music provides the emotion.

There is also a visual dimension. We create virtual singers to represent the players and observers, placing them in settings inspired by the time and location of the original game. These are actors rather than photographic reproductions of the historical players. The result is an entertaining chess lesson, more on the entertainment side than on the side of serious analysis but you experience the game in a refreshing and new way.

Creating music comes with one utterly hopeless challenge: finding a style that appeals to everybody. Musical taste is almost a declaration of social identity. A seasoned musician might happily wander from Renaissance madrigals to dark trap hip-hop, while others recoil the moment the music leaves their stylistic comfort zone. So for our first game of the World Championship between Sindarov and Gukesh we chose some modern main stream radio sound, a mixture of melodic rap and indie pop:

The second game. How to turn a short draw into a baroque pop opera?

And this is a page of other musicals that cover the great classics. Here you will find a bigger variety of musical styles:

https://radio.chessbase.com/musicals

There you either click on single musicals or chose the titles/games you like and let them run in a loop for a nice demo in any kind of chess gathering.

AI Slop? Of course! Many people today are wary of the tidal wave of AI-generated content of all kinds. And rightly so. A machine cannot be an artist. But it can help us experiment with fresh ideas without investing huge amounts of time and effort, and playfully venture off the beaten path with a little tongue in cheek.
